story:
Milan put on his warm coat. Snowy flakes fell outside the arena. Inside, it was big and loud.

Milan liked to watch the basketball players. They jumped so high. "How do they get so tall?" he asked Dad.

Dad pointed to a wall. It had marks for tall kids. "Let's see how tall you are." Milan stood by the wall. The mark was low, under yesterday's line. "That's funny," said Milan. "I measured this morning. The line was higher. Did I shrink?"

Dad smiled. "Stand up very straight." Milan stood straight as a stick. The mark stayed low. "It is because it is night," Milan said slowly. "In the morning I am a tiny bit taller. At night I am smaller. What makes that happen?"

Dad tapped his own back. "See how I bend after standing all day? You will be tall again tomorrow." Milan wondered about that. He liked being tall in the morning.

The buzzer rang. The game began. A player in yellow ran past. A bee was on his shirt, a big black and yellow bee. "I like that bee!" Milan said. He stood on his seat to see. The tall player bounced the ball. It went in the net. "He is tall now," said Milan. "But in the morning, he is a tiny bit taller." Dad laughed. Milan waved his bee hands and cheered.

Peyton loved music day at school. Today they would bake bread first. Then they would sing a new song. Ms. Kim let Peyton stir the dough. "Sugar goes in," said Ms. Kim. "And this little bit of yeast too." Peyton stared at the bowl. The yeast looked like tiny dust. How could dust do anything? The class went to the rug to sing. The song was about a horse. A big, silly horse who jumped over the moon. Peyton had to sing the high part. The first time, her voice went squeak, squeak, like a mouse. "Sing high like the horse jumps," said Ms. Kim. Peyton jumped a little as she sang. Her voice went high. It worked. Then Peyton smelled something warm. She ran to the bowl. The dough was big now. It was puffed up like a pillow! "It grew because the yeast ate the sugar," said Ms. Kim. "The yeast made little bubbles of gas." Peyton leaned close. Pop, pop, went the tiny bubbles, like the dough was humming. "The dough is singing too," Peyton said. She sang her high part again, and the dough rose up to meet her, higher and higher, like a big bread horse getting ready to jump.

Theodore ran to the culture fair with his dad. A big map hung on the wall. "I want to visit every country in one summer!" Theodore said. A girl named Priya laughed. "There are about 195 countries in the world," she said. "That is a lot of suitcases."

Theodore frowned. Then he saw the stamp table. Each table was a different country. He made a rule. "First, pick a table. Next, get a stamp. Then, find it on the map. Last, draw a red dot." He started at Russia. "This one is the biggest," Priya said. "It stretches across 11 time zones." Theodore drew a very big dot.

Next they walked to the Vatican City table. A boy was looking for it on the map. "Where is it?" he asked. Theodore found the tiny spot. "It is the smallest country," Priya said. "You could walk across it in about 20 minutes." The boy was surprised. "My walk to school takes longer than that!" he said. Everyone laughed.

Theodore matched his stamps to his red dots, one by one. Twenty dots done. His hand was cold from the frost on his cup of juice. "Only 175 more countries to go," said Dad. Theodore grinned. "Maybe next summer too." Priya gave him a high five. Then Theodore put one more red dot on the map.

Elliot walked into his new classroom. He saw blocks, paints, and a big rug. His teacher, Ms. Bell, had a job for everyone. "Measure the rug," she said. "Tell me how long it is."

Elliot walked heel to toe along the rug. He counted his steps out loud. "Fourteen footsteps!" he said. His new friend Dora measured too. She counted her steps. "Eleven," she said.

They both looked at each other. "The rug can't be two lengths," said Elliot. Dora frowned. "Maybe we counted wrong. Let's try again." They measured again. Elliot got fourteen again. Dora got eleven again.

Ms. Bell came over. She did not tell them the answer. She just handed Elliot a ruler. "Try this," she said. Elliot lined the ruler up along the rug. He moved it along, one length at a time. Dora did the same. They both got the same number. "Our feet are different sizes," said Dora. "That's why we got different answers."

The ruler used the same marks every time, so the answer matched. Later, at snack time, Dora sprinkled crumbs on the table like frost on a window. Elliot laughed. "Your hands are useless at eating crackers," he said, and they both giggled. "Ruler race after snack?" said Dora. Elliot picked up his ruler and ran.

Owen was trying to make a wall pocket for his art supplies, but the paper strips kept sliding off the cardboard border no matter how much tape he used. His loyal dog, Biscuit, trotted in from the yard with a burr tangled in her fur. Owen tried to pull it off, and it clung tight.

"Ow, Biscuit, why won't you let go?" he asked. He held the burr up close and squinted at it. Little hooks, like a hundred tiny fingers, curled out of the seed. Was that how it grabbed on so well? He pressed the burr against his wool sleeve and felt it catch. His first attempt to make a strap this way used one burr and a scrap of fuzzy sock, and it held two crayons together without any tape at all.

Maybe hooks and fuzz were better than glue. Owen spent the afternoon stitching a strip of hooked burr seeds along the top of his wall pocket and a strip of fuzzy sock along the wall. He counted the burrs, then doubled the sock fuzz so every hook would find a loop. Then he pressed the pocket to the wall and stepped back.

It stayed. It even held his heaviest marker box. Owen grinned and patted Biscuit's head.

"You're not just a dog," he told her. "You're my helper engineer." Biscuit wagged and shook loose one last burr, right onto his drawing.

Henry's cousin Marco had promised him something daring, and Henry could hardly sit still on the wooden dock. Today was the Festival of Boats in the old city of Venice, Italy, where the priest blessed every vessel that floated past the ceremony stage. Gondolas drifted by with ribbons on their prows. Bells rang. The air smelled of salt, wet wood, and somebody's fried dough nearby, which made Henry's stomach growl so loudly that a grandmother beside him laughed.

"Look, look!" Henry pointed. A boy about his own age rowed toward the dock, his boat heaped with bundles of letters and bread. Henry had been sorting the passing boats all morning, by size and by color, by whether they carried people or cargo. But this one puzzled him. A delivery boat? He had always pictured delivery kids pedaling bicycles with baskets. Where were the bicycles here? Where were the cars, the trucks, the mail vans? He scanned the streets behind the dock and saw only narrow stone lanes and footsteps.

"Marco, there are no roads at all!" Henry whispered. Marco grinned. "More than 100 islands, all stitched together with bridges," he said. Henry's mind raced. That explained the ambulance boat he had spotted earlier, painted white with a red cross, sliding down the canal. Of course! No roads meant everything, mail, groceries, even emergencies, traveled by water. The delivery boy wasn't odd. He was exactly right for this city. It was like discovering that pigeons and whales were both mammals, in a way, the same kind of thing but shaped for different worlds.

"Combine your boat with mine," Marco suddenly said, "and you could carry the whole festival." Henry laughed, imagining a mega-boat stacked with bread, bells, and one loud grandmother.

When the delivery boy rowed close, Henry waved. "Can I try one stroke?" he called. The boy tossed him the oar. Henry gripped it, pulled hard, and wobbled the boat in a circle while everyone cheered.

"Hold on tight," the boy shouted, "and row like you mean it!"

The community center's music room smelled like old carpet and lemon cleaner, and Dylan sat in the corner chair hugging the cello like it might escape. He had signed up for the Saturday orchestra voluntarily, which now seemed like a decision made by a completely different boy, one who had never seen a page full of tiny black dots sitting on lines like ants on a fence.

"Okay," said Marisol, the girl next to him, tuning her own cello. "That's an A. Play yours and we'll match."

Dylan dragged his bow across the string. The sound came out wobbling and sad, like a goose with a cough. Marisol winced. "Try again. Just persevere through the squawk stage. Everybody squawks."

"Even you?"

"Especially me. My dog used to leave the room."

He tried again, and this time the note landed close to hers, and something in his chest went warm. The concept of reading music was still a mystery, though. The dots on the page were supposed to tell him which string and which finger, but they might as well have been a secret code from another planet.

After practice, the two of them walked home the long way, over the old train bridge. They liked to stand there and drop pebbles into the creek. Dylan leaned against the rail to rest the cello case, and his elbow touched the cold metal.

Buzzzzz.

He froze. "Marisol. Did you feel that?"

"Feel what?"

"Put your ear on the rail. Carefully." She gave him a look like he had suggested licking the bridge, but she bent down and pressed her ear against the steel. Her eyes went wide.

"It's humming," she whispered. "Like a giant phone on vibrate."

Dylan pressed his ear next to hers. The rail sang, a low steady note. Then, much later, a sound came through the air, faint and growing: the rumble of a train, still far down the line. The rail had known first. The rail had known before the air did.

"Sound travels faster through the rail than through the air," Marisol said slowly, like she was testing each word.

"So the rail heard the train way before we did." Dylan sat back on his heels, thinking. "That's why your cello sounds different when you press it against the floor, isn't it? When you were tuning, I could feel your A in my chair."

Marisol's mouth dropped open. "Test it. Play your A and I'll touch your cello."

He lifted the cello out of its case right there on the bridge, set the bow, and played his A, still a little wobbly but true. Marisol pressed her palm flat against the wood.

"I feel it!" she shouted over the wind. "It's buzzing in my hand!"

The train rumbled underneath them and the whole bridge hummed along, and Dylan laughed out loud. "See? The bridge is in the orchestra too." He played the A one more time, and this time it didn't squawk at all.

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like cinnamon and burnt sugar, which meant one thing: the fudge had failed again. Anthony stood at the counter with five glass bottles lined up in a row, each filled to a different height with water, because Grandma had promised him that if he figured out her old bottle instrument, he could keep it. She tapped a spoon across them in order, and out came a rising scale, low to high, as the bottles went from full to empty. "See? Simple," she said, patting his shoulder on her way to rescue the fudge pan.

That was the problem. It wasn't simple. Anthony wanted to play "Happy Birthday" for Grandpa tomorrow, and he could only make it work if he understood the pattern, not just memorized it. So while Grandma scrubbed the pan and hummed to herself, he tapped each bottle again, listening hard. He hypothesized that less water made the note climb, and it seemed true, over and over, like a rule he could finally trust.

Then he tried showing off for his cousin Maya, who arrived with her overnight bag and zero patience for spoons. "Just blow across the tops," she said, like everyone on earth knew that. Anthony wet his lips, blew across the fullest bottle, and braced for the lowest note of the set. Instead it came out high and reedy, almost squeaky. Maya laughed so hard she snorted. He tried the nearly empty bottle next, and it hummed out a deep, round tone.

"That's backwards," Anthony said, staring at the bottles as if they had lied to him on purpose. "Full is supposed to be low. It was low this morning." He lined them up and blew across all five in order, and the scale ran in reverse, high to low, exactly opposite to the tapping. Maya said, "Maybe the bottles are haunted," and Grandma, without turning from the stove, said the fudge was probably haunted too.

Anthony sat with his chin in his hands. Two patterns, both real, both coherent, both pointing in opposite directions, depending on how you played. He filled a sixth bottle halfway between two others and predicted its notes both ways before testing: when he tapped it, the note landed between the pair; when he blew, it landed between them too, but from the other direction. The rule worked. He couldn't have explained it to a science teacher, but he didn't need to; he needed it to play a song.

The next evening, Anthony stood in the dining room while Grandpa tried to guess what his presents were. Anthony took a breath and blew across the bottles in an order that felt completely wrong and sounded completely right, and "Happy Birthday" came out whole and sweet. Grandpa clapped before the last note faded, and Grandma slipped Anthony a square of fudge, "the unhaunted batch." Maya raised her water glass and said, "A revolution in music, one backwards bottle at a time," and Anthony took his bow.

Zoey sat at Priya's kitchen table with her chemistry book open to a page full of hexagons, the shapes her teacher called ring structures. Priya was at the stove, stirring a pot of rice, and their project on organic molecules was due Monday, but somehow the rice had become the more interesting problem.

"It's been twenty minutes and it's still crunchy," Priya said, tipping the lid to show the hard little grains rolling around in the water. "I make rice all the time. I don't get it."

Zoey leaned over the pot. The water was bubbling gently, nothing like the rolling boil her own mother demanded at home. She remembered a fact from the chapter she'd skimmed the night before, half asleep: water's boiling point depends on air pressure. At twice normal pressure, like inside a pressure cooker, water boils at about 120 degrees Celsius and food cooks faster. On a high mountain, water boils well below 100 degrees.

"Priya, is the lid on tight?"

"It's on. It's just, the lid doesn't fit that pot. It kind of floats." Priya demonstrated. The lid rocked on the rim, letting steam hiss out around the edges.

"Okay, so here's a thought." Zoey turned off the burner for a moment so they could think without the noise. "If the lid sealed, the pressure inside would build up. That's what a pressure cooker does. Twice the pressure and the water boils at 120 instead of 100. Your lid doesn't seal, so all the steam escapes, and the water never gets past its regular boiling point. The rice is cooking at 100 when it wants, basically wants, more."

Priya looked at her, then at the pot, then at the drawer by the sink. "My mom has that heavy pot with the clamping lid. The scary one."

They found it in the bottom cupboard, a squat aluminum thing with a swinging lock that moved like a pendulum, ticking from side to side before it caught. Priya poured the half-cooked rice into it, clamped the lid, and set it on the burner. Within minutes the valve began to hiss steadily and the whole pot trembled faintly.

"Is it supposed to do that?" Priya asked.

"I think the hissing is the point. That's the extra pressure. Well, some of it." Zoey checked the clock. When they opened it eight minutes later, the rice was soft all the way through, each grain separate and tender, and Priya took a bite straight from the pot and closed her eyes.

"That's the fastest rice of my life," she said.

"Because it was cooking at 120 degrees. Hotter water, faster rice." Zoey felt a small, private satisfaction, the kind that came from changing one thing and watching the result. Then a memory surfaced, her uncle's stories from his camping trip in the mountains last summer, complaining for an entire phone call that his rice stayed hard no matter how long he boiled it. She had assumed he was just a bad cook. Now she pictured him at his high campsite, his little pot bubbling away at well under 100, and she started to laugh.

"What?" Priya asked.

"My uncle. On the mountain. All those weeks of crunchy rice, and it wasn't him." Zoey reached for her phone. "I have to call him before he plans another trip. He's going to argue with me, and then I'm going to explain about the pressure, and he's going to feel so much better about himself."

Hunter had been staring at the same twelve lines of Python for ten minutes when Marcus slid his chair over and looked at the screen. They were in Marcus's kitchen, because Marcus's mom didn't care if two boys took over the table on a Saturday, as long as they kept the volume down and the snacks off the keyboard. Hunter's program was supposed to ask for a name and print a greeting, but every time he ran it, Python just blinked at him like he'd said something rude.

"You're missing the parenthesis at the end of line eight," Marcus said, tapping the screen without actually touching it. "Happens to me like five times a day."

Hunter fixed it, ran the program again, and there it was, his greeting, plain and correct. He felt a small, private flash of triumph, the kind he suspected nobody ever admitted to out loud. Then Marcus said he'd found a practice site with beginner problems, and pulled it up on his own laptop so they could work through a few together. Hunter had to make an account first, so he typed in a username and a password, some quick improvised string of letters he made up on the spot because he didn't want to use a real one on a random website.

They solved three easy problems, the kind where you print a pattern of stars and feel like a genius. Then Hunter wanted to log in on Marcus's laptop too, and couldn't remember his improvised password, so he clicked the forgot password link. The email arrived fast. When he opened it, the message said, here is your password, followed by the exact password he'd typed.

Marcus went still. "That's bad."

"It's convenient," Hunter said.

"No, think about it. That site still knows my password is what I typed." Marcus's older sister was always going on about this stuff, and apparently some of it had rubbed off. "The good sites don't keep your password. They keep a scrambled version of it, and the scrambling only goes one way. That's why everywhere else sends you a reset link instead of emailing the actual thing."

Hunter wasn't sure he believed it, mostly because he didn't want to. He liked the convenience. But he'd spent all morning learning that a program does exactly what you tell it, no more, and exactly what its data allows, no less, so he decided to test the idea the way he'd test code: change one thing, watch what happens. He reset his password on the practice site to a new made-up string, waited, then clicked forgot password again. A minute later, there came the new password, plain as a handshake, sitting in his inbox like it had been waiting politely the whole time. The site was doing it both times. It wasn't luck. It was the way the site was built.

"Okay," Hunter said slowly. "So if they ever get broken into, whoever does it gets everybody's passwords, just like that."

"Like the site handing them a gift bag," Marcus said. His tone stayed cordial, but he was already closing the tab, unhurried and deliberate, like a doctor who's seen the antibody fail and knows exactly what's spreading. "You should use a different password everywhere from now on. Especially there."

Hunter deleted the account from the login screen, then opened his own notebook and wrote the rule down at the top of a fresh page, underlining it twice. Then he went back to line eight and added the parenthesis before he could forget.

The program was only eleven lines long, and Nathaniel had typed nine of them correctly, which was the maddening part. Dhruv's basement smelled like microwave popcorn and old carpet, and the desk lamp buzzed at a pitch Nathaniel could hear only when the house went quiet, which it did whenever Dhruv's mother went upstairs. On the screen, the simulation was supposed to flip a coin a hundred times and print every streak of five in a row. Instead it printed nothing at all.

"You're sure it compiles," Dhruv said, leaning over Nathaniel's shoulder with the particular authority of someone who had finished the tutorial two weeks earlier and had not written anything since.

"It compiles. It runs. It just doesn't find any streaks." Nathaniel scrolled through the output again, as though the streaks might be hiding. He had flipped a real quarter on Dhruv's desk while waiting for the code to build, out of pure fidgeting, and gotten five heads in a row, which he'd assumed meant the quarter was cheating on his behalf. Now the machine insisted such things never happened. One of them was lying, and machines were not supposed to lie, which meant the machine was telling the truth about the wrong thing.

He read the loop out loud, tracing it with a pencil Dhruv kept for math homework. "Count goes up when the flip matches the last one. Count resets when it doesn't. Print when count hits five." Then he stopped, pencil hovering, and asked the question he'd been circling: was the bug in the counting, or in the printing? He tested the counting explanation by adding a line that printed the count after every single flip. Numbers spilled down the screen, and there, plain as anything, the count climbed to five and kept climbing, six, seven, and still nothing printed. So the counting worked. Which meant the flaw was hiding somewhere he hadn't looked, and he'd been assuming the two explanations were equally likely when the evidence was already pointing at one of them.

Dhruv found it, sort of, by accident, sprawling back in his chair and saying, "Wait, why is there a semicolon after the if?" Nathaniel stared at it. A single semicolon, sitting at the end of the condition line like a period at the end of a question, making the whole if statement a do-nothing. "That's the print guard," he said, half to himself, half to the lamp. "The condition's fine. It's just not connected to anything." He deleted one character, ran it again, and the screen filled with streaks: a run of six heads around flip twenty, two separate runs of five tails, one monster run of seven. A hundred flips, and the thing found streaks everywhere, as though the coin couldn't help itself.

That was the part that snagged him. He flipped the real quarter again, watching it, and thought about his own certainty earlier that five heads in a row meant the next one had to be tails, that the coin owed him balance. But the program's coin had no memory of the previous flip; each one came up on its own, and still the streaks came, long ones, just because a hundred tries gives streaks room to happen somewhere. He wondered how many other things he'd decided about the world from short runs of bad luck, whether the week that wrecked his midterm grades had implicated his whole study method or was just a run in a longer sequence. The two ideas sat side by side and refused to merge: each event alone, and patterns everywhere in the long count. He couldn't prove anything about his own life from it, he decided, the sample was too small, and he laughed at himself for even trying.

Dhruv, who had been watching this whole silent reckoning with the expression of someone witnessing a math haunting, said, "You look despondent over a coin."

"I'm not sad, I'm amazed," Nathaniel said. "I deleted one semicolon and the universe started working." He saved the file twice, which he now considered basic hygiene, and typed a new line at the top: change the number of flips from a hundred to a thousand. "Want to see how long the streaks get?"

Dhruv dragged his chair closer. "Run it."

Antoine had been staring at the same four lines of code for eleven minutes when Ms. Okafor's third-period programming class began to smell like the rain outside, wet jackets drying against the radiators. The assignment was simple in the way that simple things are not: write a program that asks for a person's age and prints whether they can vote. His program kept telling seventeen-year-olds they could not, which was true of no one in the room except him, and he could not find the error.

"Check your equals signs," said Priya from the next computer, without looking up from her own screen. She said it the way people say check your fly, kindly but tired of saying it.

He checked. He had written one equals sign where he wanted two, so instead of comparing age to eighteen, he was telling the computer that age was eighteen, and then asking whether eighteen was greater than or equal to eighteen, which the computer answered no, because he had also written the comparison backwards. Two errors stacked on top of each other like wet jackets. He fixed the first one, ran the program, and got a different wrong answer, which somehow felt worse than the original wrong answer. Debugging, he was learning, was less like fixing a machine and more like arguing with someone who took everything you said with perfect literalness and had no interest in your intentions.

At lunch he sat with his phone, the way he always did, thumbing through his feed while eating the dry rectangle the cafeteria called pizza. Somewhere between a video of a man eviscerating a movie he had never seen and a video of two strangers screaming at each other about sneakers, he noticed that his thumb had stopped moving on its own, that he had watched the screaming one twice, and that his jaw was set tight enough to ache. He scrolled further and found another argument, then another, each louder than the last. He put the phone face down on the table, which he did not usually do, and looked out the window at the parking lot.

"You good?" said Marcus across from him, who was eating fries one at a time like they were expensive.

"Yeah. My feed's just mad at me today."

"Feeds don't get mad."

Antoine considered this. "No," he said. "But it knows I watch the angry stuff longer. That's the only thing it knows about me." He turned the phone back over and scrolled, deliberately this time, counting. Watch time, he thought, was the only measurement the thing had, and anger made him watch. It was almost tautological: the app showed him what kept him watching, and what kept him watching was what made him unable to look away. The feed wasn't trying to make him furious. It was trying to make him measurable, and fury happened to be very measurable.

Fifth period was study hall, which for Antoine meant the library, which meant the corner table where the vending machine hummed a low G. He opened his laptop to finish the voting program and found himself instead sketching something in his notebook: a loop, one of the first things they had learned. Show content, measure the watch, show more of what was watched. He wrote the loop out in pseudocode, then in the real syntax, then looked at it. It was clean. It was elegant, even. It was also, if you fed it human attention, a machine for finding the worst possible version of a person and handing it back to them.

He understood, sitting there, that he could not decide which half of himself to trust. The half that wanted to build the loop because it was beautiful and correct, or the half that wanted to throw his phone into the lake by the athletic fields. His uncle called his major-to-be "epistemology problems," by which his uncle meant: how do you know what you know, and who told you. Antoine had always thought that was a college word for something that would never apply to him. Now he had written a five-line program that knew him better than he knew his own lunch order, and it knew only one fact about him, and that fact was a clenched jaw.

He could ask whether the program was wrong. But the program wasn't wrong; it did exactly what he'd told it to, like the voting program had, and the errors had all been his. That was the uncomfortable symmetry. The feed wasn't broken either. Somebody had written it correctly, for a definition of correct that he now understood he had never actually agreed to.

After school he walked out past the buses, stopped, and opened the voting program one more time. He typed his own age into the prompt, pressed enter, and watched the terminal print, in letters he had positioned himself, "You can vote." He looked at it for a while, the rain stopped and the lot half empty, then closed the laptop and put it in his bag. Tomorrow he thought he might write a different loop, one that counted something else.

The laptop was his grandfather's, which meant it weighed roughly as much as a paving stone and made a sound like a small airplane taking off. Elijah settled it on the kitchen table between a bowl of cherry tomatoes and a stack of unopened mail, cracked his knuckles, and opened the tutorial his roommate-to-be had sent him. September was two months away. Two months to learn enough Python that he wouldn't be the only kid in the lecture hall who had never written a line of code.

"Print," his grandfather said, reading over his shoulder. "You need a machine for that?"

"It's a command. Print, parenthesis, quote, hello world, quote." He hit enter and the words appeared in the terminal, glowing green against black. Elijah actually laughed out loud, alone in his grandmother's kitchen, at a program that had taken him four seconds to write. It felt like a magic trick where he was both magician and audience.

His grandmother drifted in with a watering can and peered at the screen. "Hello, world," she read slowly, and patted his shoulder. "Very polite. Better than most of the internet."

That was the thing, though. The internet was mostly what he was thinking about, because the tutorial's next chapter included a sidebar, a little boxed paragraph he almost skipped, about history. The first web page had gone online in 1991 at CERN, and in 1993 Tim Berners-Lee, the inventor, persuaded the lab to release the underlying technology royalty-free. Elijah read the sentence twice. Free. It could have been licensed, metered, owned, the way basically everything online was now, and instead one guy at a physics lab talked the whole institution into giving it away.

"Grandpa," he called. "Did you know the web could have been a paid product?"

His grandfather was in the garage doing something mysterious to a lawnmower, and his answer came back muffled and equivocal, something that contained the words "Al Gore" and possibly "golf." Elijah let it go. He sat with the fact instead, turning it over the way you turn over a stone to see what's underneath.

Because here was his real problem, the one that had been bothering him since he'd committed to a computer science minor in a moment of career panic. He had been approaching coding like a vault to crack: learn the syntax, collect the credential, get the job. That was the version of things his guidance counselor had valorized for two straight years,STEM, salary tables, LinkedIn, as though the point of learning was the invoice at the end. But the sidebar sat there contradicting all of it. Berners-Lee gave it away. The whole substrate of modern life, released royalty-free, on the persuasive strength of one person's conviction that open beats owned. Elijah felt an unexpected flick of foreboding mixed with genuine thrill, the specific vertigo of realizing the world you'd been living in had been a coin flip.

He tried to get back to the lesson. Variables. That part was fun; x equals 5, then x equals x plus 3, and the machine just agreed, no argument, which was more than could be said for anyone in his family. But then he typed "3" instead of 3, and the program broke. Strings, integers, some distinction the tutorial explained with a metaphor about a wolf in sheep's clothing that made everything worse. Elijah stared at the error message, which said TypeError and nothing else useful, like a fortune cookie written by a lawyer. He almost texted his roommate-to-be, Dev, who was clearly some kind of prodigy, and then decided no. Debug it yourself. It was his own bug, his own responsibility, the kind of small sovereignty the tutorial kept calling "thinking like a programmer."

He found it in eleven minutes, which felt like eleven hours, and when the little program finally ran, adding his grandmother's age and his grandfather's age and announcing the total in cheerful green type, he raised both fists over his head like he'd won something. His grandmother, who had wandered back in, said, "One hundred and fifty-eight. We're antique." She laughed at the machine's earnestness, at the way it presented the sum of their years as though it were news.

Elijah saved the file. Then, because the idea wouldn't leave him alone, he opened a new file and wrote a comment, a note to himself the machine would ignore: "the web went free in 1993. could have gone the other way." He didn't know yet what he thought about that, whether he believed open systems survived because they were better or just because he wanted them to be, whether he was learning a trade or joining a tradition or both at once. That stayed uncertain, and he let it. But he typed it anyway, one small line of code standing on ground that somebody, thirty years ago, had decided to leave public.

"Earth to Elijah," his grandmother said, setting down the watering can. "There are tomatoes with your name on them."

"Coming," he said, and hit run one more time, just to watch the green words blink into being.
